title: One Hit Inherited, One Hit Rare

scenes.tts: A child inherits one broken copy of a gene called R B one. That broken copy sits in every cell of the child. So why is the whole eye not a tumor? Most such children develop only a few tumors, mostly in the retina, and often in both eyes.
scenes.caption: A child inherits one broken copy of a gene called RB1. That broken copy sits in every cell of the child. So why is the whole eye not a tumor? Most such children develop only a few tumors, mostly in the retina, and often in both eyes.
scenes.visual: One cell with two chromosome 13 bars, one red broken copy, one green working copy; it multiplies into a grid of identical cells; three cells turn tumor-orange with a question mark.
scenes.narration: A child inherits one broken copy of a gene called RB1. That broken copy sits in every cell of the child. So why is the whole eye not a tumor? Most such children develop only a few tumors, mostly in the retina, and often in both eyes.

scenes.tts: The inherited mutation is only the first of two steps. A cell has two copies of the gene, and one working copy usually gives enough brake on growth. So a tumor needs a second hit that removes the working copy. That second hit is rare. It strikes only a few cells, and only those cells become tumor.
scenes.visual: Same grid. A yellow second hit strikes the green bar of a few cells; the bar turns red and the cell turns orange; the other cells stay unchanged.
scenes.narration: The inherited mutation is only the first of two steps. A cell has two copies of the gene, and one working copy usually gives enough brake on growth. So a tumor needs a second hit that removes the working copy. That second hit is rare. It strikes only a few cells, and only those cells become tumor.

scenes.tts: Now count the second hits. Assume each tumor comes from an independent second hit. Say a carrier averages one and a half tumors per eye. The number of tumors then follows a Poisson curve. The chance of no tumor in one eye is zero point two two three. The chance of at least one is zero point seven seven seven.
scenes.caption: Now count the second hits. Assume each tumor comes from an independent second hit. Say a carrier averages 1.5 tumors per eye. The number of tumors then follows a Poisson curve. The chance of no tumor in one eye is 0.223. The chance of at least one is 0.777.
scenes.visual: Poisson bars for a mean of 1.5 tumors per eye; the zero bar is marked 0.223; the other bars are bracketed as at least one, 0.777.
scenes.narration: Now count the second hits. Assume each tumor comes from an independent second hit. Say a carrier averages 1.5 tumors per eye. The number of tumors then follows a Poisson curve. The chance of no tumor in one eye is 0.223. The chance of at least one is 0.777.

scenes.tts: Take both eyes together, and assume the eyes are independent. Tumors in both eyes: about sixty percent. A tumor in one eye only: about thirty-five percent. No tumor in either eye: about five percent. So about ninety-five percent of carriers get a tumor. That fraction is called penetrance.
scenes.caption: Take both eyes together, and assume the eyes are independent. Tumors in both eyes: about 60%. A tumor in one eye only: about 35%. No tumor in either eye: about 5%. So about 95% of carriers get a tumor. That fraction is called penetrance.
scenes.visual: Three columns, each with a pair of eyes above a bar: both eyes 60.4 percent, one eye 34.7 percent, none 5.0 percent; a bracket over the first two reads 95 percent, penetrance.
scenes.narration: Take both eyes together, and assume the eyes are independent. Tumors in both eyes: about 60%. A tumor in one eye only: about 35%. No tumor in either eye: about 5%. So about 95% of carriers get a tumor. That fraction is called penetrance.

scenes.tts: Now a child with no inherited copy. Both rare hits must fall in the same cell. Suppose the expected number of tumors per eye were zero point zero zero zero one. A tumor in each eye would then have a chance of about one in a hundred million. So these tumors are single and one-sided. They also tend to be found later, because two events must pile up in one cell line.
scenes.caption: Now a child with no inherited copy. Both rare hits must fall in the same cell. Suppose the expected number of tumors per eye were 0.0001. A tumor in each eye would then have a chance of about 1 in 100 million. So these tumors are single and one-sided. They also tend to be found later, because two events must pile up in one cell line.
scenes.visual: A cell with two green bars takes a first hit, then a second hit, and turns orange; the numbers 0.0001 and about 1 in 100 million appear; one eye with one tumor; an arrow marked later.
scenes.narration: Now a child with no inherited copy. Both rare hits must fall in the same cell. Suppose the expected number of tumors per eye were 0.0001. A tumor in each eye would then have a chance of about 1 in 100 million. So these tumors are single and one-sided. They also tend to be found later, because two events must pile up in one cell line.

scenes.tts: This resolves the puzzle. In a family, the inherited allele looks dominant. About half of a carrier's children inherit it, and most of them develop tumors. Yet inside one cell, the same allele is recessive. A pedigree follows risk. A cell counts copies. So an inherited first hit is dominant in the family and recessive in the cell.
scenes.visual: A three-generation pedigree on the left with affected people in each generation; on the right one cell with one red and one green bar that stays healthy until the second hit makes it a tumor.
